tldr: To enable quadruped robots to autonomously navigate complex terrains with parkour movements, the authors developed MulDP, a multimodal diffusion policy that integrates past visual perception, proprioception, and goal history to generate future velocity command sequences. In real-world experiments, the robot successfully tracked a dynamic target over more than 1 km across stairs and obstacles without any human intervention.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of MulDP. It encodes and fuses historical depth images, proprioception, the current depth image, historical control commands, and local goals. A diffusion model then iteratively denoises this context to generate a temporally coherent future velocity command sequence.
overview:
Thanks to advances in deep reinforcement learning, motion control for quadruped robots has made remarkable progress, enabling challenging parkour skills such as jumping and climbing ledges. However, most existing systems still rely on human teleoperation for high-level navigation—deciding where to go and at what speed. Conventional autonomous navigation methods either focus solely on avoiding obstacles or output only sparse waypoints like wheeled robots do. As a result, they struggle with fine-grained velocity regulation (such as building up momentum before a jump) and cannot handle the dynamic physical constraints specific to legged robots.

To solve this, the authors proposed MulDP (Multimodal Diffusion Policy), which frames navigation velocity command generation as a conditional diffusion generation process. MulDP uses separate encoders to extract features from time-series depth images, proprioception such as joint angles, current spatial terrain features, and recent decision history alongside goal information. Conditioning a diffusion model on these combined features allows it to output future velocity command sequences that respect dynamic physical constraints. To support training, the authors also created QPND, the first large-scale parkour navigation dataset built in Isaac Sim.

In both simulation and real-world experiments using a Unitree Go1, MulDP achieved an 89.7% success rate, significantly outperforming existing visual navigation baselines. Furthermore, in real-world outdoor tests, the robot autonomously navigated over 1 km following a dynamic target without human intervention, seamlessly combining stair climbing, gap leaping, hurdle jumping, and avoiding unknown obstacles.
contributions: Developed MulDP, a multimodal diffusion policy that integrates historical visual perception, proprioception, and decision history to generate temporally coherent and anticipatory velocity command sequences.
Constructed and released QPND, a large-scale simulation dataset for quadruped parkour navigation using only a forward-facing depth camera and onboard sensors.

Demonstrated high success rates in fixed-goal navigation across diverse terrains (including stairs and gaps) and achieved over 1 km of autonomous parkour target tracking without human intervention on a real Go1 robot.

sections.heading: The Challenges of Autonomous Parkour and the Goal of MulDP
sections.summary: While quadruped agility skills have advanced rapidly, autonomous navigation to guide such locomotion across complex terrains remains underexplored. The authors propose a diffusion-based navigation policy to achieve tight perception-action coupling and velocity regulation tailored to physical dynamic constraints.
sections.details:
In recent years, reinforcement learning has empowered quadruped robots to master advanced parkour behaviors like running, leaping, and climbing. However, many existing studies still depend on human teleoperation to choose travel directions and speeds. Fully autonomous parkour navigation across complex environments has remained largely unaddressed.

Standard navigation for wheeled robots focuses primarily on bypassing obstacles without collision. In contrast, robot parkour demands long-horizon, anticipatory velocity regulation—such as accelerating ahead of time to build up momentum for leaping across a gap. In addition, an open path visible in camera frames may be impassable depending on leg length and physical geometry. This creates a significant gap between visual traversability and actual embodied traversability.

Traditional map-based planners separate mapping, planning, and control, making fine-grained dynamic velocity modulation difficult. Meanwhile, learning-based methods that only output target endpoints or waypoints cannot provide the fine continuous control commands that legged robots need. End-to-end reinforcement learning and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models also face high training costs and generalization hurdles over long horizons.

To overcome these issues, this paper introduces MulDP, formulating navigation command generation as a conditional diffusion process. By leveraging the expressive representation power of diffusion models to capture multimodal action distributions and temporal dependencies, MulDP achieves real-time, terrain-adaptive autonomous parkour navigation.

sections.heading: Diffusion Policies in Robotics and the Limits of Current Visual Navigation
sections.summary: While diffusion policies have shown remarkable success in robot manipulation, applying them to quadruped parkour has been hindered by a lack of datasets and tailored model architectures. This work tackles these gaps with specialized encoders and a dedicated simulation dataset.
sections.details:
### II-A Advances in Robot Diffusion Policies
A longstanding challenge in robot policy learning is handling multimodal action distributions and strong temporal correlations where multiple valid paths exist. Traditional Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and Energy-Based Models (EBMs) have limitations in expressiveness and scalability, whereas diffusion models can approximate arbitrary distributions. In particular, Diffusion Policy in robot manipulation demonstrated that iteratively denoising action sequences directly from observations yields smooth and stable control. However, its adoption in quadruped parkour navigation has lagged due to the absence of large-scale multimodal datasets and architectures capable of handling whole-body dynamics and temporal lookahead.

### II-B Limitations of Visual Navigation Models
Visual navigation without prior maps has also been widely studied, with recent models incorporating foundation models (e.g., ViNT) and diffusion techniques. However, most existing approaches only output the next waypoint or a target heading angle. While adequate for wheeled platforms, this is insufficient for quadrupeds that must rapidly switch between acceleration, jumping, and deceleration depending on terrain. Moreover, conventional visual navigation treats obstacles purely as things to avoid, failing to exploit the quadruped's natural ability to traverse or leap over barriers. MulDP breaks through these limitations by tightly coupling proprioception with vision to directly generate executable continuous velocity commands.

sections.heading: MulDP Architecture and the QPND Parkour Dataset
sections.summary: MulDP consists of three specialized encoders—capturing temporal visual-proprioceptive features, current spatial features, and action history—paired with a diffusion model. It is trained on QPND, a custom dataset of diverse terrain traversals collected using only standard onboard sensor specifications.
sections.details:
### III-A System Overview
The overall structure of MulDP is shown in Figure F1. It fuses forward-facing depth images, onboard proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.), and recent decision history to predict a future velocity command sequence $U_t$ via a diffusion model. The first step of the generated sequence is sent to a low-level locomotion policy, with replanning repeated at 5 Hz.

### III-B Dataset Generation (QPND)
To facilitate smooth Sim-to-Real transfer without assuming expensive extra sensors like LiDAR, the authors built QPND in Isaac Sim using only a forward-facing depth camera matching an onboard RealSense D435i (field of view, 10 Hz, 2 m max range) and proprioception.
- **Terrain Composition**: Traversable terrains include gaps (width 0.4–0.7 m), hurdles (height 0.4–0.5 m), and stairs (step height 0.15–0.2 m), alongside non-traversable obstacles (width 0.3–1.0 m, height up to 1.0 m).
- **Low-Level Policy**: A reinforcement-learning-based parkour locomotion policy, RENet, handles low-level joint execution.
- **Trajectory Collection**: Basic terrains were collected automatically using scripted controllers, while challenging terrains with multiple viable solutions were gathered via human expert teleoperation. The dataset contains 31.0 km across 6,400 trajectories and roughly 250,000 depth frames.
- **Data Augmentation**: Trajectories were segmented into short contiguous clips (boosting reuse by 50%), depth borders were cropped, and 1% random depth noise alongside Gaussian noise (variance 0.01) was added to mimic real sensor imperfections.

### III-C Diffusion Policy Network Architecture
The policy comprises three encoders and a noise prediction network:
1. **Multimodal Temporal Encoder ($Enc_{h1}$)**: Splits the last 5 frames of depth images ($44 \times 56$) into $4 \times 4$ patches (154 tokens) and feeds them into a Transformer alongside 45-dimensional proprioception to produce a 128-dimensional spatio-temporal feature $h_1$.
2. **Current Spatial Encoder ($Enc_{h2}$)**: To react to sudden obstacle appearances, a shallow CNN processes only the latest depth frame in parallel, extracting fine local spatial features $h_2$.
3. **Decision Memory Encoder ($Enc_{h3}$)**: An MLP processes the last 5 control inputs and the local goal vector to produce $h_3$, preserving navigational intent and geometric consistency.
Conditioned on this concatenated context $c_t$, a 4-layer, 4-head DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model) network $\epsilon_\theta$ refines pure Gaussian noise over 10 denoising steps to generate the future velocity command sequence $U_t = \{(\Delta v_{t+i}, \Delta \theta_{t+i})\}_{i=0}^{H-1}$.

### III-D Model Training
Training is performed end-to-end via supervised learning on clean trajectories and noise sampled from QPND, minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between predicted and injected noise. Optimization uses AdamW (learning rate $10^{-4}$) with a batch size of 512 for 1,000 epochs.

sections.heading: Simulation and Real-World Experiments: 89.7% Success Rate and 1 km Traversal
sections.summary: MulDP achieved an 89.7% success rate in benchmark evaluations, clearly outperforming existing baselines. Ablations confirmed the critical role of proprioception and noise injection. In real-world tests, it demonstrated anticipatory acceleration before gaps and generalized zero-shot to bypass unknown obstacles across a 1 km run.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted using a Unitree Go1 across six terrain types in Isaac Sim: Gap, Hurdle, Upstairs, Downstairs, Gravel, and Box across two difficulty levels. Metrics include Success Rate (SR, reaching within 0.2 m of the goal), Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), Traversed Area Ratio (TR), and Time to Reach (TTR). Real-world experiments ran on an onboard NVIDIA Orin NX at a 5 Hz inference rate.

### IV-B Baseline Comparisons and Ablations (Addressing Q1)
As shown in Figure F2, MulDP achieved a **Success Rate (SR) of 89.7%** and an **SPL of 71.9%**, significantly outpacing the retrained diffusion baseline NavDP* (SR 59.0%) and ViNT* (SR 71.5%). The original pre-trained NavDP (SR 38.4%) and ViNT (SR 35.8%) exhibited overly conservative obstacle avoidance and failed to traverse parkour terrains.

Ablation studies highlighted several key takeaways:
- **Removing Proprioception (w/o Prop)**: SR dropped sharply from 89.7% to 69.5%, demonstrating that sensing body posture and joint states is vital for parkour navigation.
- **Removing Decision Memory (w/o DME)**: SR collapsed to 7.4% (while TR remained high at 90.3%, indicating aimless wandering). History is crucial for goal convergence.
- **Data Augmentation & Depth Noise**: Without augmentation (w/o DA), SR plummeted to 32.5%. As shown in Figure F3, omitting depth noise injection (w/o DN) caused the robot to misjudge obstacle heights due to real-world sensor noise and collide, whereas MulDP successfully climbed over the box.

### IV-C Fixed-Goal Task and Velocity Profile Analysis (Addressing Q2)
In an unseen $16\text{ m} \times 16\text{ m}$ environment (Figure F4), MulDP exhibited clear multimodality, generating diverse and safe paths between identical start and goal points. Looking at real-world velocity profiles (Figure F6), the robot autonomously accelerated its forward velocity to nearly 2.0 m/s right before a gap to build momentum, decelerating smoothly after landing. Around tight obstacles, it smoothly increased its angular velocity to slip through without abruptly stopping, avoiding unnecessary loss of kinetic energy.

### IV-D Dynamic Target Tracking Task (Addressing Q3)
In outdoor dynamic tracking experiments (Figure F5), MulDP completed **over 1 km of fully autonomous parkour navigation** without any human intervention. It continuously tackled stairs, grass, gaps, and hurdles. Furthermore, as illustrated in Figure F7, when encountering unseen obstacles like a ground disc on grass or an abandoned bicycle, MulDP correctly identified them as impassable and steered around them safely, proving strong zero-shot generalization.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: MulDP makes autonomous parkour navigation for quadrupeds a reality using a multimodal diffusion policy. Future work will focus on semantic terrain understanding, integration with global path planners, and lightweight safety fallback modules.
sections.details:
This work proposed MulDP, a multimodal diffusion policy, and QPND, a dedicated parkour dataset, to achieve autonomous parkour navigation for quadruped robots.

By tightly integrating forward depth visual observations, onboard proprioception, and past decision history, MulDP produces temporally coherent velocity command sequences. Rather than simply detouring around every obstacle, the robot autonomously chooses aggressive traversal actions like leaping gaps, ascending stairs, and jumping over hurdles. Its robustness was confirmed across both simulation and real-world trials, including outdoor traversals exceeding 1 km.

Promising directions for future work include incorporating semantic terrain understanding, coupling the policy with long-range global path planners, and adding lightweight safety evaluation modules to handle real-world failsafes.

takeaways: For high-agility parkour navigation, directly predicting temporal velocity command sequences—which allow anticipatory acceleration before jumps—is far more effective than outputting sparse geometric waypoints.
Integrating proprioception alongside visual inputs is essential for robots to judge embodied traversability and achieve high navigation success rates.
Sim-to-real transfer succeeds reliably without external LiDAR by applying depth noise injection and trajectory segmentation augmentations during simulation training.
limitations: Relies on a high-precision Ultra-Wideband (UWB) positioning system for dynamic target tracking and localization; operating in environments without GPS or UWB will require dedicated onboard state estimation.
Lacks semantic perception, limiting the ability to discern material risks that cannot be deduced from geometry alone (e.g., distinguishing between a solid step and a puddle or fragile cardboard).
Running iterative diffusion denoising inference (10 steps at 5 Hz) introduces computational load and latency challenges when deployed on small onboard compute units like the Orin NX.
